ai-at-work.title: Claude Cowork finally remembers what you told the app in chat
ai-at-work.excerpt: Anthropic is giving Claude a shared memory across chat and Cowork, so users no longer have to repeatedly brief the AI on projects, preferences, and other context.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic rolled out memory features for Claude so the AI can now retain what you've told it across different conversations and workspaces instead of making you repeat yourself every single time. This matters because digital workplace tools that actually remember context save enormous amounts of time and reduce the friction of working with AI assistants throughout your day. Honestly, it's wild this took this long to ship, but I'll take it. We've spent thirty years complaining that enterprise software doesn't understand our work. Finally, an AI vendor gets the memo.

ai-at-work.title: OpenAI’s Jalapeño chip is built for fast inference at scale, benchmarks show
ai-at-work.excerpt: Tested on SemiAnalysis’ InferenceX benchmark, Jalapeño registered both more tokens per user and more throughput per kilowatt than the currently available state-of-the art.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: OpenAI built a custom chip called Jalapeño that processes AI responses faster and more efficiently than existing hardware, according to benchmark testing. This matters because digital workplaces are about to deploy way more AI assistants and copilots, and cheaper, faster inference means better user experiences and lower infrastructure costs for your organization. Of course, this assumes OpenAI actually ships the thing at scale and doesn't get distracted by the next shiny project, which in tech is always a big assumption.

ai-at-work.title: ‘The world seems to be ready’: An interview with OpenAI head of product Thibault Sottiaux
ai-at-work.excerpt: TechCrunch talks agents, UX, and reporting to Greg Brockman with OpenAI's head of product.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: OpenAI's head of product is talking about AI agents and user experience design as the company plots its next moves under Greg Brockman's leadership. This matters because whatever OpenAI ships next will inevitably end up in your enterprise tech stack whether you asked for it or not, and understanding their product philosophy helps you prepare for that reality. Look, I've been doing this thirty years and I've learned one thing: when a company with this much cash and confidence says "the world seems ready," they're usually talking about their readiness to ship something, not the world's actual readiness to use it.

ai-at-work.title: Claude Code costs up to $200 a month. Goose does the same thing for free.
ai-at-work.excerpt: The artificial intelligence coding revolution comes with a catch: it's expensive.Claude Code, Anthropic's terminal-based AI agent that can write, debug, and deploy code autonomously, has captured the
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic's Claude Code charges up to $200 monthly for AI-assisted coding while Goose offers identical functionality for free, triggering pushback from developers over pricing. For digital workplace pros managing developer tools and budgets, this matters because AI coding assistants are becoming table stakes for productivity, and cost structures this steep will either drive adoption of cheaper alternatives or force conversations about ROI with finance teams. Here's the thing: in 30 years I've watched tech companies repeatedly price themselves out of their own ecosystems, and a $200 monthly tab for something free exists next door is exactly how you lose developer mind share.

tools-tech.title: Anthropic's Claude and Cowork will share memories about you now - unless you opt out
tools-tech.excerpt: Anthropic is merging Claude chat and Cowork memory, raising privacy questions about what AI remembers and if it's worth the tradeoff.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Anthropic just merged Claude and Cowork so the AI remembers details about you across both platforms, but you have to actively opt out to stop it. This matters because most digital workplace tools are heading this direction, and if your employees are using Claude for work, the company now has a persistent profile of their interactions and preferences unless someone clicks the right box. The real question isn't whether AI remembering stuff is cool (it obviously is for convenience), but whether your organization has actually read the privacy docs to know what's being stored and who can see it.

tools-tech.title: I ditched T-Mobile for Mint and found 3 major drawbacks of smaller carriers - and their workarounds
tools-tech.excerpt: Downsizing from a 'big three' carrier can save you big money, but it has its downsides. Here's how I'm adapting to them.
tools-tech.dwp_take: A tech journalist switched from T-Mobile to Mint Mobile and discovered that smaller carriers have real limitations around coverage, customer service responsiveness, and network prioritization during congestion. This matters to digital workplace folks because many of us are hybrid workers relying on mobile connectivity as our lifeline, and saving fifty bucks a month doesn't help if you're dropping calls during client presentations. The honest takeaway: there's no such thing as a free lunch in telecom, and sometimes paying for the big player's network stability is just the cost of doing business when your livelihood depends on staying connected.

tools-tech.title: How I turned my ancient Windows PC into a Chromebook for free - with FydeOS
tools-tech.excerpt: FydeOS aims to bring a Google Chromebook-like experience to standard PCs, and it succeeds - with a caveat or two.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Someone took an old Windows machine and installed FydeOS to make it run like a Chromebook without spending a dime. This matters because IT departments are always hunting for ways to extend hardware lifecycles and reduce the cost of device refreshes, especially when budget season rolls around. Here's the thing though: before your CFO gets too excited about this magic bullet, remember that "mostly works" is the digital workplace equivalent of "the parachute mostly opened."

tools-tech.title: Perplexity’s on-device AI offering promises data control and lower token costs
tools-tech.excerpt: Perplexity on Tuesday rolled out an offering that runs the AI entirely on a local machine, and that, it said, will keep “private data local and escalating to the cloud only when a task needs it.” The
tools-tech.dwp_take: Perplexity launched Portable Computer, an on-device AI that keeps data local and only sends it to the cloud when necessary, running on Nvidia hardware with their own trained models. For digital workplace teams drowning in data governance requirements and token costs, this matters because it offers a genuine alternative to shipping everything to some vendor's servers. The timing is perfect since every enterprise IT leader I know is simultaneously terrified of data breaches and exhausted by their cloud AI bills, so a solution that addresses both is refreshing, even if the hardware requirements will keep it out of most people's hands for now.

digital-culture.title: Job recruiters are failing Gen Z job seekers
digital-culture.excerpt: The road to employment continues to get longer for Gen Z job seekers as they experience a frustrating job market. Data from the U.S. Census Bureau and U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics shows that in Jun
digital-culture.dwp_take: Recruiters aren't connecting with Gen Z applicants effectively, leaving recent grads with unemployment rates hovering around 5.7 percent while younger workers overall sit at 7.2 percent. This matters because your talent acquisition strategy is probably built on outdated channels and messaging that simply don't reach this generation where they actually spend time. Here's the thing: if your recruiting process still looks like it did in 2015, Gen Z will ghost you faster than you can say "synergy," and honestly, you deserve it.

industry-news.title: Uber Fined $966M: The High Cost of Automation Without Oversight
industry-news.excerpt: Uber faces a $966 million Dutch privacy fine over automated driver suspensions, raising questions about GDPR compliance and meaningful human oversight. The post Uber Fined $966M: The High Cost of Auto
industry-news.dwp_take: Uber got slapped with a $966 million fine in the Netherlands for automatically suspending drivers without proper human review or explanation, which violates GDPR requirements. This matters because it shows regulators are finally calling out companies that treat automation as a substitute for actual governance and accountability. If you've been telling your leadership that "the algorithm handles it" is not a compliance strategy, you just got an expensive Dutch vindication.

industry-news.title: Taiwan Indicts Nine Over Alleged Nvidia AI Server Smuggling to China
industry-news.excerpt: Taiwan indicted nine people, including Nvidia and Super Micro staff, over an alleged scheme that diverted restricted AI servers to customers in China. The post Taiwan Indicts Nine Over Alleged Nvidia
industry-news.dwp_take: Nine people, including employees from Nvidia and Super Micro, have been indicted in Taiwan for allegedly smuggling restricted AI servers to China in violation of export controls. This matters to digital workplace pros because it highlights how serious governments are getting about protecting advanced technology infrastructure and the compliance risks your organization faces if you're sourcing or managing enterprise hardware. The real takeaway here is that "we didn't know" is no longer a defense, so if your company is buying enterprise gear, you need to actually know where it's coming from and where it's going.

industry-news.title: Microsoft Teams’ New Policy Lets Admins Automatically Block Meeting Bots
industry-news.excerpt: Microsoft Teams is adding a policy that lets IT admins automatically block detected external meeting bots instead of relying on organizer approval. The post Microsoft Teams’ New Policy Lets Admins Aut
industry-news.dwp_take: Microsoft is giving Teams admins an automatic kill switch to block external meeting bots without waiting for organizer sign-off. This matters because security teams have been losing sleep over unauthorized bots joining calls and potentially siphoning data, while organizers often approve things without thinking twice. Finally, IT gets to be the grown-up in the room instead of hoping everyone reads the security email they definitely didn't read.

industry-news.title: Apple Tests AI Shopping Assistant in Store App: What Can It Do?
industry-news.excerpt: Apple is testing an AI shopping assistant in the Apple Store app that can answer product, trade-in, payment, and order questions for select users. The post Apple Tests AI Shopping Assistant in Store A
industry-news.dwp_take: Apple is quietly testing an AI shopping assistant in their Store app that answers questions about products, trade-ins, payments, and orders for a limited group of users. This matters to digital workplace folks because it shows how enterprise companies are embedding AI into customer-facing systems to handle routine inquiries, which means your own organization is probably getting pitched this exact same capability right now. Here's the thing though: if Apple can't make their AI assistant less annoying than their current in-store experience, we're just trading one frustration for another.
